question: Can an interactive dashboard built from many axis-aligned one-dimensional loss slices, conventional two-dimensional slices, interpolation paths, and Hessian directions give users a faithful and interpretable view of a small fully connected network's high-dimensional loss landscape?

key_findings.claim: FuNNscope is a substantial linked-view prototype for tiny networks, but its main axis-parallel view is a finite set of coordinate sections rather than a global geometric reconstruction.
key_findings.evidence: The dashboard links the network graph, target and predicted surfaces, loss history, target points, sampling points, per-parameter slice charts, random two-dimensional planes, linear paths, and Hessian-eigenvector curves. Each grey curve in a slice chart varies one parameter while fixing all others at one focus point. Those curves exactly expose sampled coordinate sensitivity, but they do not determine off-axis values, diagonal interactions, basin connectivity, or the geometry outside the chosen bounded ranges. The paper's phrases 'global perspective' and 'truly global view' therefore exceed the represented object.

key_findings.claim: The slice axes are readable parameter coordinates, but that readability is not invariant to neural-network symmetries or reparameterization.
key_findings.evidence: A chart axis names one raw weight or bias, so it is more directly readable than an unnamed random direction. Yet hidden units can be permuted without changing the represented function, and common rescalings can change coordinate curvature while preserving predictions. The paper cites Dinh et al.'s warning about flatness and says swapped-weight minimizers retain a similar general geometry, but it supplies no quotient, alignment, permutation test, or function-space comparison. Consequently, layer and weight 'influence' can reflect the selected parameterization rather than an intrinsic model property.

key_findings.claim: Sampling multiple focus points includes interaction effects in individual function evaluations, but it does not solve the curse of dimensionality or establish approximation fidelity.
key_findings.evidence: At a focus point, changing one coordinate evaluates the full network with all other coordinates fixed, so interactions with that particular setting affect the curve. However, the paper gives no reconstruction rule, error bound, coverage statistic, convergence study, or held-out comparison with the true landscape. Its showcased global experiment uses 500 Sobol focus points, 31 parameters, and 81 samples per slice, nominally 1,255,500 forward-loss evaluations, for a model with only 31 parameters. Coverage becomes exponentially sparse as dimension grows even before the number of displayed curves becomes unmanageable.

key_findings.claim: The empirical scope is one 31-parameter sigmoid regressor on one synthetic function, so observations cannot validate transfer from toy networks to deep models.
key_findings.evidence: All three use cases share a 2-4-3-1 fully connected sigmoid network with 31 parameters, trained by MSE on 256 random samples of sin(x)+sin(y) over [0,5]^2. The figures examine the zero vector, selected minima, and one gradient-descent trajectory in that same setup. There is no second architecture, activation, dataset, objective, seed-level quantitative replication, convolutional or residual model, or modern-scale experiment. The abstract explicitly assumes that small-network observations can generalize, but the paper does not test that assumption.

key_findings.claim: The zero-vector patterns are visually clear but partly arise from a singular, deliberately bad initialization rather than evidence about a general loss landscape.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 11-12 show a flat central region and different layerwise coordinate shapes around the all-zero parameter vector. The authors themselves note that zero is usually a bad initialization and explain that equal zero weights and sigmoid saturation drive the observed patterns. With all downstream weights zero, many hidden-layer perturbations cannot affect the output to first order. No nonzero initialization ensemble or analytic baseline is used to determine which patterns are generic rather than consequences of this special point.

key_findings.claim: The minimizer views expose coordinate-specific sensitivity, but they do not establish sharpness, stability, generalization, or full-space basin structure.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 13-14 show random-plane funnels, leading-Hessian-direction curves, and 31 coordinate charts around a selected solution with loss 0.04. Some weights have visibly steeper coordinate curves than others, which is a valid local diagnostic in the chosen coordinates. But no perturbation-to-prediction metric, test-set gap, symmetry-normalized sharpness, confidence interval, comparison across independently trained solutions, or off-axis escape test is reported. A coordinate-wise minimum can still be a saddle or connect to a low-loss path in another direction.

key_findings.claim: The claim that optimization navigates high-loss obstacles is not demonstrated by the displayed interpolation and coordinate slices.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 16 shows a high barrier on a straight line from an Adam start to endpoint, while Figures 17-19 show coordinate sections along a separate batch-gradient-descent trajectory. A straight-line interpolation barrier does not imply that the actual path faced that obstacle, and target points sitting near minima of individual coordinate slices do not establish a multivariate valley or identify off-axis barriers. The paper acknowledges that the remaining descent direction lies off-axis, but offers no trajectory overlay in a common subspace, path-loss comparison, counterfactual optimizer, or barrier-crossing measurement.

key_findings.claim: The visualization encodings introduce known perceptual and numerical risks that the interface exposes but does not resolve.
key_findings.evidence: Hundreds of overlapping grey curves require opacity and zoom controls; all four study participants found the sampling menu and slice charts overwhelming or hard to interpret. Natural splines make sparse samples appear smoother and can invent values between evaluations, a risk the paper explicitly says should be taken 'with a grain of salt.' Random two-dimensional plots are regenerated with different directions and are implemented without Li et al.'s normalization filters, weakening visual comparability. Figure 1's dense dashboard and Figures 14, 17, and 19 also show that small labels and repeated panels become difficult to scan even at 31 parameters.

key_findings.claim: The four-person formative evaluation yields a mean SUS of 69.375, but it does not validate scientific interpretability or task performance.
key_findings.evidence: One physicist and three computer scientists received a tutorial and free exploration. Individual SUS scores were 65.0, 67.5, 70.0, and 75.0, whose mean is 69.375; three of four thought the prototype could be useful, while four of four found the core slice interface overwhelming or difficult. There were no defined diagnostic tasks, correctness labels, completion times, comparison tools, counterbalancing, qualitative coding protocol, preregistered hypotheses, or uncertainty estimates. The study is valuable design feedback, not evidence that the charts support reliable landscape conclusions.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not provide a reproducible released system or an end-to-end performance budget in the reviewed revision.
key_findings.evidence: The implementation names JavaScript, D3, vis-graph3d, PyTorch, and hessian-eigenthings, and gives several model and sampling settings. It does not provide a FuNNscope code or data URL, immutable artifact, browser/backend protocol, dependency versions, random seeds, training batch details, exact optimizer settings for every figure, latency, memory, caching strategy, or total run times. The final page says the authors are still in the process of making the web tool available. Hessian views additionally contradict the broad suggestion that only forward propagation is needed for the complete dashboard.

method.core_idea: Make the parameter axes themselves interpretable by displaying, for every weight and bias, an ensemble of one-dimensional loss curves obtained around many sampled network states, then link those curves to standard loss-landscape and training views in one interactive dashboard.
method.mechanism: A user builds a tiny fully connected model and two-dimensional regression target, trains one or more runs, and selects a target parameter vector such as initialization, zero, an intermediate checkpoint, or a minimizer. The system samples focus points around that target using uniform, Sobol, or mixed sampling. For each focus point and each parameter coordinate, it varies only that parameter over a chosen interval, evaluates the forward loss, and overlays the resulting curve in the coordinate's chart. Linked views show the sampled points, target-point metadata, network graph, predictions, training history, random two-dimensional loss planes, linear interpolation paths, and one-dimensional slices along Hessian eigenvectors.
assumptions: A bounded finite ensemble of coordinate slices is representative enough to support conclusions about global high-dimensional geometry.
Raw parameter coordinates remain meaningfully comparable despite neuron permutation, scaling, activation, and other reparameterization symmetries.
The selected focus-point distribution covers rare but important basins, barriers, saddles, and interactions.
Patterns from a 31-parameter sigmoid regressor transfer to deeper and structurally different networks.
Visual judgments of symmetry, flatness, funnels, obstacles, and sensitivity are stable across viewers and plotting settings.
Opacity, zoom, common axes, and optional splines preserve rather than distort the evidence in dense curve bundles.
Coordinate-wise minima along a trajectory reflect multivariate valleys and optimizer behavior.
Random two-dimensional planes remain comparable without filter- or layer-wise normalization.
Users can manage the D charts and D times focus-point sampling cost for the intended model size.
Forward-loss access is sufficient for the slicing component, while differentiability and a Hessian implementation are available for the eigenvector component.

techniques.role: Creates nearby or broad parameter vectors with uniform, Sobol, or mixed sampling around a selected target.
Varies one raw weight or bias at a time and overlays the resulting loss curves for many focus points.
Coordinates network, prediction, sampling, loss-history, target-point, and landscape panels through shared selections.
Evaluates a conventional two-dimensional random-direction slice around a selected parameter vector.
Plots training and test loss along a straight interpolation between two saved target points.
Plots one-dimensional loss curves along approximate Hessian eigenvector directions.
Treats saved training states as target points and compares their coordinate slices over optimization.
Mitigates overplotting through common scales, curve opacity, and per-chart zoom.
Lets users trade exact piecewise-linear samples for a smoother but interpolated visual curve.

evaluations.setting: One 2-4-3-1 sigmoid regressor with 31 parameters and 256 random samples of f(x,y)=sin(x)+sin(y) on [0,5]^2.
evaluations.metric: Visual inspection of linked prediction, slice, interpolation, random-plane, and Hessian-direction plots.
evaluations.result: The dashboard displays coherent qualitative patterns around zero, selected minima, and training checkpoints.
evaluations.baseline: No second task or architecture, numeric fidelity target, ground-truth landscape reconstruction, or competing interface is evaluated.

evaluations.setting: Global zero-vector view with six random planes plus 500 Sobol focus points in [-5,5], each of 31 coordinates sliced over [-25,25] at 81 samples.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative central flatness, symmetry, layer similarity, and low-loss slice density.
evaluations.result: Random planes and coordinate charts show a flat-looking center; last-layer coordinates look more parabolic and few sampled slices reach loss below 1.0.
evaluations.baseline: No nonzero initialization ensemble, analytic toy-model reference, coverage estimate, or uncertainty across sampled focus sets.

evaluations.setting: Selected trained solution with loss 0.04, shown through 31 coordinate charts, random two-dimensional planes, leading Hessian directions, and output surfaces.
evaluations.metric: Visible coordinate curvature and qualitative funnel shape.
evaluations.result: Different coordinates show visibly different local sensitivities, and prediction surfaces improve as selected loss falls from 0.36 to 0.04.
evaluations.baseline: No symmetry-normalized sharpness, test generalization, functional robustness, repeat-minimum distribution, or held-out diagnostic decision.

evaluations.setting: Batch gradient descent at learning rate 0.01 from weights uniform in [-5,5], with early checkpoints every epoch and late checkpoints 1,000 epochs apart.
evaluations.metric: Loss reduction and positions of checkpoints within coordinate slice charts.
evaluations.result: Displayed loss falls from 4.89 to 1.63 over the first 50 epochs and from 0.57 to 0.06 in later stages; later checkpoints often sit near coordinate-wise minima.
evaluations.baseline: No common-subspace trajectory, optimizer comparison, descent-direction overlay, barrier-crossing metric, or repeated-run statistic.

evaluations.setting: Formative free-exploration study with one physicist and three computer scientists after a tutorial PDF.
evaluations.metric: System Usability Scale and open-ended feedback.
evaluations.result: SUS scores 65.0, 67.5, 70.0, and 75.0 average 69.375; three of four saw possible utility, while all four found the sampling menu and slice charts overwhelming or hard to interpret.
evaluations.baseline: No task-based accuracy, completion time, comparison visualization, counterbalancing, inferential statistic, or representative-user sample.

limitations: Author-stated: the method is intractable for networks with millions of parameters and the displayed chart count becomes difficult to manage.
Author-stated: overlapping curves, varying slice density, scale choice, and low sample resolution make slice charts hard to read.
Author-stated: natural splines guess unsampled loss values and must be interpreted cautiously.
Author-stated: the four participants found the core sampling and slicing views overwhelming or hard to interpret.
The primary evidence uses one 31-parameter sigmoid architecture, one synthetic regression function, and one broad experimental storyline.
A finite collection of axis-aligned one-dimensional sections is not a global representation and has no reported approximation error.
Raw coordinate geometry is not invariant under common neural-network permutations and reparameterizations.
The showcased 500-by-31-by-81 configuration already implies about 1.26 million loss evaluations before scaling beyond 31 parameters.
Random planes omit the normalization filters used by the cited Li et al. baseline.
The user study evaluates formative usability, not correctness or scientific diagnostic value.
No FuNNscope artifact, code release, runtime, memory budget, or hyperparameter-complete reproduction protocol appears in the reviewed revision.
The optimizer-obstacle conclusion relies on separate straight-line and coordinate-section plots rather than evidence in a shared multivariate subspace.
failure_modes: Important diagonal interactions or narrow basins fall between focus points and never appear in any coordinate chart.
A neuron permutation makes the same represented function appear under different chart labels and undermines cross-model comparison.
A scale-preserving function reparameterization makes one coordinate look arbitrarily sharp or flat.
Opacity hides rare high- or low-loss curves, while full opacity turns the chart into an unreadable band.
Natural splines introduce visually persuasive extrema or smooth passages that were never evaluated.
Random two-dimensional directions and missing normalization change a plot more than the model difference being compared.
A point that is minimal along every displayed coordinate direction still has an off-axis negative-curvature or low-loss escape direction.
A straight interpolation exhibits a barrier even though a short curved low-loss connection exists.
The zero-vector singularity dominates conclusions that do not recur around ordinary random initialization.
The number of curves and forward evaluations grows beyond interactive latency long before modern parameter counts.
Dashboard density, small labels, and inconsistent chart scales cause viewers to select visually salient rather than scientifically relevant patterns.
Users infer optimization causality from retrospective plots without an intervention or common trajectory representation.
reusable_insights: Label a view by the exact sampled object—coordinate sections around focus points—rather than calling it the global landscape.
A landscape atlas should make sampling support, unobserved regions, and approximation uncertainty visible alongside the curves.
Raw parameter sensitivity should be paired with symmetry-aligned or function-space perturbations before comparing weights or models.
Use linked target points and brushing across training, prediction, parameter, and landscape views; this integration is FuNNscope's clearest reusable design contribution.
Keep exact samples visually distinct from interpolated curves, and never let smoothing fabricate unmarked evidence.
Treat sampling evaluations, latency, memory, and display density as explicit scalability metrics rather than future-work footnotes.
Validate a visualization with task accuracy and decision quality, not only SUS and free-form preference.
Compare coordinate slices with mode connectivity, Hessian spectra, topology, and nonlinear embeddings because the methods answer different local-versus-global questions.
For optimizer claims, render the actual trajectory and counterfactual paths in one stable aligned subspace and measure the maximum loss encountered.
Progressively disclose slice summaries, clusters, outliers, and selected curves instead of initially drawing every curve in every parameter panel.
open_questions: What quantitative reconstruction or diagnostic error does an ensemble of coordinate slices achieve on functions whose full landscape is computable?
How many focus points are required as dimension, interaction order, slice range, and desired rare-basin recall change?
Can active sampling target high-interaction or uncertainty regions with far fewer than D times focus-points times resolution evaluations?
How should parameter axes be aligned or quotiented across neuron permutations, scaling symmetries, and independently trained models?
Do coordinate-slice patterns predict training failure, generalization, robustness, or optimizer choice on held-out models?
Which summaries preserve the useful outlier curves while keeping hundreds or millions of parameters navigable?
Can functional perturbation axes retain human meaning while avoiding raw-coordinate artifacts?
Does a common trajectory-aligned subspace support more accurate optimizer-barrier judgments than independent coordinate slices?
How much information do slice charts add beyond Hessian eigenvalues, gradient norms, random planes, and mode-connectivity metrics at matched compute?
Would expert users complete preregistered landscape-diagnostic tasks more accurately with FuNNscope than with LossPlot, Neuro-Visualizer, LossLens, or a simple small-multiples baseline?
Can a multiscale interface connect tiny exact coordinate views to topological summaries and global relationships among many trained solutions?

competitive_landscape.title: Qualitatively characterizing neural network optimization problems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational predecessor for linear loss interpolation from initialization to a trained solution.
competitive_landscape.difference: Goodfellow, Vinyals, and Saxe use a simple one-dimensional diagnostic to test for optimization obstacles across several networks. FuNNscope embeds that diagnostic in a linked interface and adds per-coordinate ensembles, but its later barrier interpretation still inherits the limitation that a straight path is not the actual optimizer trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
competitive_landscape.relationship: Critical predecessor showing that parameter-space sharpness and geometry can change under function-preserving reparameterizations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Dinh et al. provide the symmetry counterexample that limits intrinsic interpretation of raw coordinate curvature. FuNNscope cites the concern but still labels coordinate-slice differences as layer and weight influence without quotienting or function-space controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets
competitive_landscape.relationship: Canonical direct predecessor for one- and two-dimensional neural loss slices and normalized cross-model comparison.
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. introduce filter-wise normalization and test architecture and training choices on convolutional and residual networks. FuNNscope adds an interactive linked system and readable raw-coordinate axes for tiny MLPs, but explicitly renders its two-dimensional plots without those normalization filters and has much narrower empirical breadth.

competitive_landscape.title: Loss Surfaces, Mode Connectivity, and Fast Ensembling of DNNs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Global-connectivity alternative that searches curved low-loss paths between independently trained modes.
competitive_landscape.difference: Garipov et al. directly optimize paths and test their training and test performance on CIFAR and ImageNet. FuNNscope can display straight interpolation and local coordinate sections but cannot establish whether distant modes are connected in the full parameter space.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring the Geometry and Topology of Neural Network Loss Landscapes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Predecessor using targeted trajectory sampling, nonlinear PHATE embeddings, and computational homology.
competitive_landscape.difference: Horoi et al. try to sample optimizer-relevant regions and quantify trajectory topology, trading away raw parameter axes. FuNNscope prioritizes exact coordinate labels and direct curves but provides neither nonlinear global embedding nor a topology or fidelity statistic.

competitive_landscape.title: Taxonomizing local versus global structure in neural network loss landscapes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Broad empirical predecessor separating local smoothness, representation similarity, and global connectivity metrics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. systematically study thousands of models and distinguish local from global landscape structure. FuNNscope offers richer inspection of one toy model but calls local and bounded coordinate evidence global without that metric taxonomy or empirical scale.

competitive_landscape.title: LossPlot: A Better Way to Visualize Loss Landscapes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous interactive-tool predecessor already cited by FuNNscope.
competitive_landscape.difference: LossPlot focuses on a simple user-driven interface for synchronously manipulating and comparing up to six supplied loss landscapes, clipping, and summary statistics. FuNNscope provides more tightly integrated model, training, sampling, and per-weight views, but only for its small-network backend and with greater interface density.

competitive_landscape.title: Neuro-Visualizer: An Auto-encoder-based Loss Landscape Visualization Method
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent nonlinear visualization competitor designed to improve low-dimensional embedding fidelity.
competitive_landscape.difference: Neuro-Visualizer learns an encoder and inverse map around training trajectories and compares linear and nonlinear baselines on knowledge-guided ML applications. FuNNscope's coordinate axes are more immediately interpretable but its finite 1D sections have no reconstruction-fidelity objective or nonlinear coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: Visualizing, Rethinking, and Mining the Loss Landscape of Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent directional-mining competitor that searches for complex one-dimensional and two-dimensional local structures.
competitive_landscape.difference: Li, Li, and Zhan actively mine directions that reveal v-side, w-basin, w-peak, and other nontrivial structures and connect them to Hessian theory. FuNNscope exhausts readable coordinate axes around sampled points but does not optimize directions for information content or validate what coordinate slicing misses.

competitive_landscape.title: Visualizing Loss Functions as Topological Landscape Profiles
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent high-dimensional summarization competitor using merge trees and topological valley profiles.
competitive_landscape.difference: Geniesse et al. compress sampled three- and four-dimensional Hessian slices into nested basin profiles, reducing dependence on one or two visible axes. FuNNscope retains direct parameter-level curves and richer interaction, but its display and sampling burden scale with every parameter and it does not summarize basin connectivity.

competitive_landscape.title: LossLens: Diagnostics for Machine Learning through Loss Landscape Visual Analytics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest subsequent visual-analytics system integrating local and global scales.
competitive_landscape.difference: LossLens links local Hessian and topological metrics with representation similarity and mode connectivity across multiple solutions, with ResNet-20 and PINN cases. It directly addresses FuNNscope's local-versus-global gap, while FuNNscope remains more granular for inspecting named weights in tiny fully connected models.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v1 (2024-12-17); IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications

competitive_landscape.title: Landscaper: Understanding Loss Landscapes Through Multi-Dimensional Topological Analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current open-source successor for arbitrary-dimensional Hessian-subspace topology and quantitative landscape diagnostics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Landscaper packages multidimensional sampling and topology, adds the SMAD smoothness statistic, and evaluates pretrained language models and chemical OOD prediction. FuNNscope's distinctive value is interactive raw-coordinate exploration, but its qualitative 31-parameter evidence and unreleased artifact do not compete on scale, quantitative validation, or current reproducibility.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first comprehensive global characterization of a neural loss landscape through axis-parallel slice charts with interpretable axes, integrated with standard landscape views in an interactive dashboard.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The reviewed revision does integrate more linked views and more named coordinate sections than its cited LossPlot and standard 1D/2D-slice predecessors, and the rendered prototype demonstrates those interactions on a 31-parameter model.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a proof-of-concept linked visual-analytics interface for dense ensembles of per-parameter loss sections in very small fully connected networks. It does not reconstruct global geometry, validate transfer to deep networks, establish scientific diagnostic accuracy, or remain state of the art after nonlinear, topological, multiscale, and open-source successors through 2026.

reviewer_notes: Read all 10 pages of the exact cached PDF, including every section, the loss definition, the displayed slice equations and parameterization, all captions, references, and all 19 figures. Rendered pages 1-10 at 150 dpi and visually inspected the actual panels: the dense linked dashboard; interpolation and random-plane examples; method diagrams; Himmelblau and Ackley slice examples; focus-sampling and opacity/spline controls; zero-vector surfaces and slices; minimizer, prediction, interpolation, and Hessian plots; early and late training slice atlases; user-study text; and references. Figure pixels were available and inspected. Primary arXiv records for direct predecessors and successors were rechecked on 2026-08-23. Numeric claims are transcribed or explicitly labeled reviewer inference; the 1,255,500 evaluation count is 500 focus points times 31 parameters times 81 samples, and the SUS mean 69.375 is the arithmetic mean of the four reported scores. No code or live FuNNscope artifact was linked in the reviewed PDF, so implementation behavior beyond the described and rendered prototype could not be tested.
